title: Given a binary array of ones and zeros and an integer k, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray containing only ones after flipping at most k zeros to ones. Solve it with the sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Longest Subarray with Ones after Replacement (Max Consecutive Ones III)
keyPoints: A variable-size sliding window counts zeros inside the window and keeps the count at most k.
When the zero count exceeds k, the left pointer advances until the budget is restored.
You never need to track which specific zeros to flip; only the count matters because all flips cost the same.
The widest feasible window seen during the scan is the answer.
Time complexity is O(N) because both pointers only move forward, and space is O(1).
This is the same sliding window template as character replacement string problems.

s1_definition.oneliner: Grow the window while the zero count stays at most k; when it exceeds k, shrink from the left until the budget is restored.
s1_definition.profdef:
- This problem asks for the **longest window** in a binary array that becomes all ones after flipping at most k zeros.
- A **variable-size sliding window** counts how many zeros lie inside the window.
- The right pointer **expands** the window; when the zero count exceeds k, the left pointer **shrinks** it.
- You only need the **count of zeros**, not their positions, because all flips cost the same.
- The widest feasible window ever seen is the answer.
- Time is **O(N)** and space is **O(1)**.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a daily on-time-payment history for a loan, where 1 means paid on time and 0 means missed. The bank's hardship policy lets him forgive at most k missed days. He wants the longest continuous clean stretch achievable after those forgiveness waivers. He slides a window across the history, forgiving misses until he runs out of budget, then tightens the left edge.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  History: [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1], k=2

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  right=0: val=1, zeros=0, window=[0,0]=1  │
  │  right=1: val=1, zeros=0, window=[0,1]=2  │
  │  right=2: val=0, zeros=1, window=[0,2]=3  │
  │  right=3: val=0, zeros=2, window=[0,3]=4  │
  │  right=4: val=1, zeros=2, window=[0,4]=5  │
  │  right=5: val=1, zeros=2, window=[0,5]=6  │
  │  right=6: val=1, zeros=2, window=[0,6]=7  │
  │  right=7: val=0, zeros=3 > k!             │
  │    shrink: left=0 (val=1), left=1         │
  │    shrink: left=1 (val=1), left=2         │
  │    shrink: left=2 (val=0), zeros=2, left=3│
  │    window=[3,7]=5                         │
  │  right=8: val=1, zeros=2, window=[3,8]=6  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Best window: [0, 6] with length 7
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the longest contiguous subarray of a binary array that becomes all ones after flipping at most k zeros, and you solve it with a variable-size sliding window in linear time using only a single counter. The right pointer advances across the array, incrementing the zero count on each zero. When the count exceeds k, the left pointer advances until the budget is restored. The widest feasible window seen is the answer.

The clarifying insight is that you never need to track which specific zeros to flip. You only need their count, because flipping any k of them costs the same. That is what collapses a combinatorial choice into a plain single-counter window, and it is why the algorithm is linear time with constant space.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this on the loan-servicing team. For each loan, the team kept a binary daily history where 1 meant the installment was paid on time and 0 meant it was missed. The hardship program allowed waiving at most k failed days in a review window. The longest continuous on-time streak achievable after those waivers determined whether the borrower qualified for a lower interest tier.

The senior-level point is that this is the same sliding window template as several string problems, just with the validity test being a zero count against k. Recognizing that shared shape lets you reuse one approach confidently across many problems, and the constant space makes it safe for streaming computation over long histories.

Remember one sentence: slide a window counting zeros, shrink when zeros exceed k, and the widest feasible window is the longest all-ones subarray after at most k flips.
